abstract: PaperOrchestra is a multi-agent framework for automated AI research paper writing.https://yiwen-song.github.io/paper_orchestra/ 🎻 PaperOrchestra: A Multi-Agent Framework for Automated AI Research Paper Writing Yiwen Song 1, Yale Song 1, Tomas Pfister 1, and Jinsung Yoon 1 1Google Cloud AI Research PaperOrchestra is a multi-agent framework for automated AI research paper writing. It flexibly transforms unconstrained pre-writing materials (ideas and experimental logs) into submission-ready LaTeX manuscripts, including comprehensive literature synthesis and generated visuals, such as plots and conceptual diagrams. Acting like an orchestrated team of specialized agents, it handles outline generation, literature review, section writing, content refinement, and plotting to close the gap between raw research materials and submission ready papers. Key Features Multi-Agent Pipeline: Orchestrates specialized agents (Outline, Literature Review, Section Writing, Content Refinement, Plotting) for end-to-end paper generation. headline: I send around PDFs and markdown files to my coworkers so much and they use their agents to make sense of the world too, so I started using this skill methodology-appendix to make sure their agents could replicate what my agents found. --- name: methodology-appendix description: "Every data-backed report or memo ends with a Methodology / Replication Appendix: the signal choice and its sensitivity, verbatim queries, derivation pseudocode over named constants, the rebuild command, and drift/limits. Appended by default, without asking." --- # Methodology / Replication Appendix ## Rule Any report, PDF or page whose conclusions rest on data queries ends with a **Replication Appendix**. It is a working recipe, not a citation list. The test: > A reader with an agent and equivalent data access can regenerate the document > end to end from the appendix alone, without contacting the author. If a reader would have to ask "which column did you use?", "what date was this pulled?" or "how do I rebuild the PDF?", the appendix failed. ## Body voice The body states conclusions plainly. No process narration ("I was asked...", "on the first pass..."), no self-grading. The first sentence after the title contains a finding. Everything about how you got there goes in the appendix at the end, written for forensic recreation. ## When this fires Always, automatically, for: - analysis memos backed by database or API queries - any PDF sent to partners, executives or external stakeholders - pages presenting quantitative findings - anything with tables of counts, rates or percentiles Skip for narrative or qualitative writing, meeting notes, personal memos, short ephemera, and documents with no data spine. Do not ask permission. ## The six sections ### 1. Header ```markdown ## Replication Appendix A reader with an agent and equivalent data access can regenerate every number and rebuild this document from this appendix alone. **Access required:** <tool/CLI + auth, internal APIs> **Snapshot date:** <ISO date>. Live-data documents won't reproduce exactly after this date; see Drift. ``` ### 2. Signal definitions and the choice that mattered The most important section. Analyses usually turn on one column or threshold choice. Name it, name the alternatives, state the impact. ```markdown ### Signal definitions | Field | What it is | Why chosen / rejected | |---|---|---| | `score_a` | Ensembled score | **Primary.** More predictive per <source>. | | `score_b` | Single-model score | Rejected as primary; kept for contrast. | | final_decision | Human decision object | Not queried. Known gap. | **Outcome sensitivity:** switching from score_b to score_a moved the headline count from N1 to N2 and changed claim X. A replication that changes the signal column will not match these numbers. ``` Always include an **Outcome sensitivity** line. If a different defensible choice changes the conclusion, the reader must know before quoting it. ### 3. Verbatim queries Every query that produced a number, copy-pasteable, in document order, labelled by the finding it supports. Never paraphrase SQL. Never write "similar to the above." Add schema notes a replicator would otherwise get wrong: enum meanings, non-obvious joins, columns that seem to exist but don't. ### 4. Derivation pseudocode Queries give raw counts; the document has derived figures. Show the arithmetic, with assumptions as named constants a reader can swap. ``` ITEMS_PER_DAY = 8 # observed median, <period> YIELD_HAIRCUT = 0.10..0.15 # marginal cases convert below observed rate gap = count(status = REJECTED and score >= threshold) extra_days = gap / ITEMS_PER_DAY added_wins = gap * YIELD_HAIRCUT ``` Different constants change the recommendation, not just the number, so they must be visible. ### 5. Rebuild command Exact commands from source markdown to verified PDF, plus a visual check (e.g. `pdfinfo` page count, `pdftoppm` a couple of pages and look at them). Name the source of record: the PDF is a render, never the original. ### 6. Drift, limits and known gaps - **Live data moves.** What was mid-flight at snapshot; what is closed and stable. - **Coverage gaps.** Fields only populated for part of the range, and how tables were restricted rather than shown with misleading denominators. - **What this cannot see.** Inputs to the real decision that the data lacks. - **Retractions.** Any claim withdrawn between versions, and why. ## Procedure 1. Log queries verbatim as you run them. Reconstructed SQL is how appendices go wrong. 2. Write the analysis. 3. Append the six sections before rendering. 4. Name the signal choice and its outcome sensitivity. 5. Render, check visually, then send. 6. On revision, update the appendix in the same commit as the finding. An appendix describing a superseded method is worse than none. ## Quality bar - [ ] Could a reader re-run this without asking me anything? - [ ] Is every headline number traceable to a pasted query? - [ ] Is the signal/threshold choice named, with alternatives and impact? - [ ] Are derived figures arithmetic over named constants? - [ ] Is the rebuild command present and correct? - [ ] Are drift, coverage gaps and retractions stated? ## Anti-patterns - **Citation theater:** table names instead of runnable queries. - **Reconstructed SQL:** retyped from memory, drifted from what ran. - **Silent signal choice:** one column presented as "the score" when a defensible alternative changes the answer. - **Buried assumptions:** constants hard-coded in prose. - **Stale appendix:** findings revised, appendix untouched. - **Asking first:** this is a default, not an offer.

The chart of token spend per employee still has no ceiling in sight. And the closer you are to AI right now the deeper the sense is that we’re actually still in the early part of the curve of token use and adoption. This summer and fall’s model releases have continued to push the state of the art forward at a rate that already felt hard to maintain. As a result, for most productive use-cases the models are only now starting to actually work, and the feeling is that things will only accelerate from here. Coding, in retrospect, was basically trash even 12 months ago. Now it’s finally starting to get good. And now that coding is actually working, you’re getting tool and computer use, which open up a wide variety of knowledge work domains that weren’t possible to throw agents at before. Once you have agents that can code, use computers, leverage any tool out there, and understand a variety of domains, you can begin to throw them at a wide variety of knowledge work tasks that were hard to bring automation to across finance, life sciences, cyber, and more. So that brings agents to a broad set of work that we’re not really using them in yet at scale. Then comes the new form factors of agents. Agent swarms and background agents are going to eat up vastly more tokens than anything we can imagine. You’ll have agents running in most enterprises workflows processing data, validating work, doing research, providing decision support, and so on. And we’ll have swarms that fan out in parallel in areas like cyber, life sciences, coding, and more. So basically tokens are only going up from here.
